es.summary: Inflamación de la mucosa nasal mediada por IgE ante alérgenos como polen, provocando congestión, estornudos y secreción clara.
key_points: Respuesta IgE desencadena liberación de histamina y leucotrienos.
Síntomas estacionales coinciden con la exposición a polen.
Diagnóstico clínico; pruebas cutáneas o IgE sérica confirman alergenos.
Tratamiento de primera línea: antihistamínicos y corticoides nasales.
Evitar el uso prolongado de descongestionantes tópicos para prevenir rinitis medicamentosa.

pathophysiology: Alérgeno inhalado se une a IgE en mastocitos de la mucosa nasal.
Activación de mastocitos libera histamina, prostaglandinas y leucotrienos.
Aumento de permeabilidad capilar produce edema y secreción acuosa.
Ciclo inflamatorio crónico genera hiperreactividad nasal.
risk_factors: Exposición frecuente a polen, ácaros o moho.
Infecciones respiratorias previas que sensibilizan la mucosa.
signs_symptoms: Congestión nasal y secreción clara acuosa.
diagnostics: Historia clínica y examen físico de la cavidad nasal.
Prueba cutánea de prick o IgE específica (valor >0.35 IU/mL sugiere sensibilización).
Descartar infección: PCR <5 mg/L y ausencia de fiebre.
treatment: Antihistamínicos orales de segunda generación (cetirizina, loratadina).
Cromoglicato de sodio nasal para prevención.
Inmunoterapia subcutánea o sublingual para alergenos específicos.
complications: Otitis media por obstrucción de la trompa de Eustaquio.
Exacerbación de asma en pacientes con enfermedad pulmonar.
Rinitis medicamentosa por uso crónico de descongestionantes.
Trastorno del sueño y disminución de la calidad de vida.
nursing_care: Evaluar patrón de estornudos, secreción y grado de congestión.
Monitorear uso y técnica de spray nasal; registrar frecuencia.
Observar signos de irritación nasal o epistaxis.
Controlar nivel de IgE si se solicita laboratorio.
Promover hidratación y uso de solución salina isotónica.
patient_teaching: Identificar y evitar alergenos desencadenantes (p. ej., polen, ácaros).
Aplicar spray nasal con cabeza ligeramente inclinada y no aspirar.
Limitar descongestionantes tópicos a máximo 3 días.
Realizar irrigación nasal con solución salina estéril 2‑3 veces al día.
Buscar atención médica si aparecen fiebre, dolor facial intenso o secreción purulenta.

related_to: uso frecuente de antihistamínicos que resecan mucosa
outcomes: Mantener integridad de la mucosa nasal sin signos de infección
Ausencia de fiebre >38°C durante el periodo de tratamiento

interventions.action: Evaluar diariamente la mucosa nasal en busca de enrojecimiento, edema o secreción purulenta.
interventions.rationale: Detección temprana permite intervención oportuna para prevenir infección.

interventions.action: Enseñar al paciente la técnica correcta de irrigación nasal con solución salina.
interventions.rationale: La limpieza mecánica reduce la carga microbiana y la irritación.

interventions.action: Limitar el uso de descongestionantes tópicos a ≤3 días y registrar la frecuencia.
interventions.rationale: Previene rinitis medicamentosa que favorece colonización bacteriana.

interventions.action: Informar al paciente sobre signos de infección (fiebre, dolor facial, secreción amarilla) y cuándo buscar ayuda.
interventions.rationale: Promueve la búsqueda temprana de atención médica.

outcomes: Realizar caminata de 30 minutos sin disnea ni fatiga
Reducir episodios de estornudos a <2 por día

interventions.action: Evaluar nivel de actividad y registrar limitaciones en cada turno.
interventions.rationale: Establece línea base para medir mejoría.

interventions.action: Administrar antihistamínicos y corticoides nasales según prescripción y observar respuesta.
interventions.rationale: Controlar síntomas mejora la capacidad funcional.

interventions.action: Enseñar técnicas de respiración diafragmática y ejercicios de apertura nasal.
interventions.rationale: Facilita la ventilación y reduce la sensación de falta de aire.

interventions.action: Planificar actividades graduales, iniciando con tareas ligeras y aumentando progresivamente.
interventions.rationale: Previene agotamiento y fomenta la tolerancia a la actividad.

interventions.rationale: Mejora la calidad del sueño y disminuye la fatiga diurna.

en.summary: Inflammation of the nasal mucosa mediated by IgE in response to allergens such as pollen, causing congestion, sneezing, and clear discharge.
key_points: IgE response triggers release of histamine and leukotrienes.
Seasonal symptoms coincide with pollen exposure.
Clinical diagnosis; skin tests or serum IgE confirm allergens.
First‑line treatment: antihistamines and nasal corticosteroids.
Avoid prolonged use of topical decongestants to prevent medication‑induced rhinitis.

pathophysiology: Inhaled allergen binds IgE on nasal mucosal mast cells.
Mast cell activation releases histamine, prostaglandins, and leukotrienes.
Increased capillary permeability causes edema and watery secretion.
Chronic inflammatory cycle generates nasal hyperreactivity.
risk_factors: Frequent exposure to pollen, dust mites, or mold.
Previous respiratory infections that sensitize mucosa.
signs_symptoms: Nasal congestion and clear watery discharge.
diagnostics: Medical history and physical exam of nasal cavity.
Skin prick test or specific IgE (value >0.35 IU/mL suggests sensitization).
Rule out infection: CRP <5 mg/L and no fever.
treatment: Subcutaneous or sublingual immunotherapy for specific allergens.
complications: Otitis media from Eustachian tube obstruction.
Asthma exacerbation in patients with pulmonary disease.
Medication‑induced rhinitis from chronic decongestant use.
Sleep disorder and reduced quality of life.
nursing_care: Assess pattern of sneezing, discharge, and degree of congestion.
Monitor use and technique of nasal spray; record frequency.
Observe for nasal irritation or epistaxis.
Check IgE level if laboratory requested.
Promote hydration and use of isotonic saline solution.
patient_teaching: Identify and avoid trigger allergens (e.g., pollen, dust mites).
Apply nasal spray with head slightly tilted and do not inhale.
Limit topical decongestants to a maximum of 3 days.
Perform nasal irrigation with sterile saline 2‑3 times daily.
Seek medical care if fever, severe facial pain, or purulent discharge develops.

related_to: frequent use of antihistamines that dry mucosa
outcomes: Maintain nasal mucosal integrity without signs of infection

interventions.action: Assess nasal mucosa daily for redness, edema, or purulent discharge.
interventions.rationale: Early detection allows timely intervention to prevent infection.

interventions.action: Teach patient correct nasal irrigation technique with saline solution.
interventions.rationale: Mechanical cleaning reduces microbial load and irritation.

interventions.action: Limit topical decongestant use to ≤3 days and record frequency.
interventions.rationale: Prevents medication‑induced rhinitis that favors bacterial colonization.

interventions.action: Inform patient about infection signs (fever, facial pain, yellow discharge) and when to seek help.

evidenced_by: shortness of breath during light activities
outcomes: Walk 30 minutes without shortness of breath or fatigue
Reduce sneezing episodes to <2 per day

interventions.action: Assess activity level and record limitations each shift.
Administer antihistamines and nasal corticosteroids as prescribed and observe response.
Teach diaphragmatic breathing techniques and nasal opening exercises.
interventions.rationale: Facilitates ventilation and reduces sensation of breathlessness.

interventions.action: Plan gradual activities, starting with light tasks and increasing progressively.
interventions.rationale: Prevents exhaustion and promotes activity tolerance.

interventions.action: Reinforce sleep hygiene: use humidifier and semi‑upright position.
interventions.rationale: Improves sleep quality and reduces daytime fatigue.

sections.pathophysiology.0.quote: If the sensitized individual is re-exposed to the same allergen, the allergen binds to the IgE antibodies on the surface of mast cells or basophils.

sections.pathophysiology.1.quote: The cross-linking of allergen with IgE antibodies on mast cells or basophils triggers the release of chemical mediators, including histamines, leukotrienes, and prostaglandins.

sections.risk_factors.0.quote: The nurse should also document the patient’s personal and family history of allergies, if any.

sections.risk_factors.1.quote: Common allergic responses are to seasonal allergens like various trees, ragweed, or pollens; medications; perennial allergens like dust or molds; latex ; animal dander; foods; household chemicals; fragrances; and insect stings or bites, as shown in Figure 24.2 .

sections.signs_symptoms.1.quote: The primary symptoms of allergic rhinitis are nasal congestion, sneezing, nose and throat itching, and abundant amounts of serous nasal drainage.

sections.signs_symptoms.2.quote: Symptoms can include: Sneezing, often with a runny or clogged nose Coughing and postnasal drip Itching eyes, nose and throat Red and watery eyes Dark circles under the eyes Your health care provider may diagnose hay fever based on a physical exam and your symptoms.

sections.treatment.3.quote: This type of medication is used prior to or at the initial onset of symptoms.

sections.treatment.4.quote: The three methods of immunotherapy include subcutaneous immunotherapy (SIT), epicutaneous immunotherapy (EPIT), and sublingual immunotherapy (SLIT).

sections.complications.4.quote: Allergic rhinitis can be severe and impedes a person’s sleep, leisure, educational or professional success, and overall quality of life.
